2027-07-09.title: First Friday of Kaitha · Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob)
2027-07-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Wonders and signs through the apostles
2027-07-09.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the longer forms Acts 19:8–20, 2 Corinthians 10:3–18 and Luke 12:1–12 and lists the day among the Commemorations of Martyrs and Saints; it prints four readings for the day (verify locally). The calendar's own headings: “I have chosen you”; “Wonders and signs through the Apostles”; “Apostles build up the Church”; “Bear witness fearlessly”.
2027-07-09.verse: do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.
theo: The first Friday of Kaitha belongs to a bishop of the border, Mar Yakob of Nisibis, James of Nisibis, who died about the year 338. Nisibis, today Nusaybin on the Turkish-Syrian frontier, stood at the edge of two empires, the Roman and the Persian, and its Christians lived under the threat of war. According to the Syriac tradition he was a man of prayer and of the Scriptures who became the first bishop of the city and the teacher of the young Ephrem, who later became the great poet and Doctor of the Church; tradition also says he took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325. When the Persian armies came against the city, the people looked to their bishop, and the Church of Nisibis remembered how her prayer, and not only her walls, had kept her. We keep his memory because we belong to the same family: our liturgy, the Qurbana of Addai and Mari, comes from the Church of the East, which had its roots in this Syriac world.

The readings give a fine frame for such a life. In Isaiah, God speaks to a small and frightened people: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen.” The name Jacob is the name of our saint, Yakob in Syriac, and it is easy to hear the promise spoken over him: “do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.” Isaiah dares to call the nation “you worm Jacob”, so small and weak, and then tells it that the Holy One of Israel is its Redeemer. The Church of Nisibis was small and exposed, and she was held by the same hand. So are we, whenever we are tired and alone: God does not choose the strong first.

In Acts the word of the Lord grows “mightily” at Ephesus, a city of magic and of the great temple of Artemis. God does “extraordinary miracles” through Paul; the sons of Sceva, who try to use the name of Jesus like a charm without belonging to him, are overpowered, and many believers confess and burn their books of magic, worth fifty thousand silver coins, before everyone. The lesson is two-sided: the name of Jesus is not a spell, and a Christian leaves the old powers openly. In Kerala some still go to astrologers, amulets and charms in time of fear; the Church asks us to put our trust in Christ alone (Catechism 2116–2117). In the Epistle Paul says that his weapons are not human: “we destroy arguments and every proud obstacle raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to obey Christ.” The weapon of a bishop is prayer, the word and the sacraments, and also patient teaching, as James taught young Ephrem. Paul adds that the authority was given “for building you up and not for tearing you down”.

The Gospel is the great word to those who bear witness. “Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.” Jesus says it to his friends, and in the same breath tells them of a Father who forgets not one of five sparrows sold for two pennies and who has counted the hairs of their head. The call to confess him is clear: “everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God.” And when they are brought before rulers, they should not worry, “for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.” The Church of the East knew this hour well; in the Persian Empire thousands of her sons and daughters were martyred in the century after Nisibis, and the Thomas Christians of India honour them in their calendar to this day. On this first Friday of Kaitha, the Friday of martyrs and saints, we ask for the same fearlessness: not the boldness of the proud, but the quiet courage of those who know that they are counted and held.
outline: A small frontier city, a praying bishop, and a God who says: do not fear.
Point 1 · Do not fear, I am with you
Isaiah's promise to Jacob the worm; the Church at the edge of two empires.
Point 2 · Not a charm, but the name
Ephesus, Sceva's sons, the burning of the books; trust in Christ alone.
Point 3 · Weapons not of this world
Paul's divine weapons; build up and do not tear down; teaching as Mar Yakob taught Ephrem.
Not one sparrow forgotten; acknowledge him; the Spirit teaches in the hour.
“Do not fear, for I am with you.”
live: If there is any amulet, horoscope or charm in your house or phone that you trust, put it away, and entrust yourself to Christ in prayer.
This week acknowledge your faith once in a quiet and respectful way in a place where it usually goes unmentioned.
Teach a child or a younger person one prayer, and pray it with them.
fathers: We multiply whenever you mow us down; the blood of Christians is seed.
It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.
magis: Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.
All forms of divination, magic and sorcery are to be rejected; they contradict the honour, respect and loving fear that we owe to God alone.
The disciple of Christ must not only keep the faith but profess it, bear witness to it with confidence, and spread it.
saints: First Friday of Kaitha: Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob), a bishop of the Syriac Church whose memory the calendar keeps among the saints. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the Church of the East. In the Latin calendar it is the Friday of the fourteenth week in Ordinary Time, with the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, martyrs of China.

7–12 July: first week and second Sunday of the Season of Kaitha. Fri 9: First Friday of Kaitha, Saint James of Nisibis (Mar Yakob). Sun 11: Second Sunday of Kaitha (in the Latin calendar the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict gives way to the Sunday). Looking ahead: Thu 15, Sts Kuriakose and Julitta; Fri 16, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-09.prayer: God our Father, you chose Jacob and told him not to fear, for you were with him. We thank you for your servant Mar Yakob, bishop of Nisibis, who taught your word, led his people in prayer and was a father in the faith to the young Ephrem. Through his intercession keep your Church safe from fear and from every false trust. Teach us to put away the charms and idols that we hold, and to place our whole trust in the name of Jesus. Give us weapons that are not of this world, the word, the sacraments and love, and strengthen all who suffer for the faith, as you strengthened the martyrs of the Church of the East. Teach us by your Holy Spirit what to say, and when we are afraid, uphold us with your right hand. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana of Addai and Mari we pray in the tradition that the Church of the East handed down, the tradition of Mar Yakob and Ephrem. The altar is where the weak are held by the right hand of God: in the Body and Blood of Christ we are given the courage not to be afraid, and in the bread and the cup we are counted and remembered, as the sparrows are counted by the Father.

quick: Isaiah: God has chosen Jacob; do not fear, for I am with you and will uphold you with my right hand.
Acts and Paul: the name of Jesus is not a charm; burn the books of magic; our weapons are divine and are for building up.
Luke: do not fear those who kill the body; not one sparrow is forgotten; acknowledge Christ, and the Spirit will teach you what to say.
2027-07-09.action: Set aside one fear this week and say to the Lord, ‘You are with me,’ each time it returns.
2027-07-09.question: In whom do I really trust when I am afraid?

family.explain: Jesus tells us that God does not forget even one little sparrow, and that he has counted every hair on our head. So we do not need to be afraid. Today we remember a bishop named Mar Yakob, who lived a very long time ago in a city called Nisibis. He prayed and taught the children, and one of his students, Ephrem, became a great singer of God's praise.
family.intention: We pray for Christians in countries where it is dangerous to say that they love Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What are we afraid of, and how can we give it to Jesus in our prayer?”

illus: A young nurse in a mission hospital in Wayanad (a story told to illustrate the reading) was afraid of the monsoon night duty: the river rose, the lights went, and a woman in labour was brought in on a jeep. Her old matron, a Sister of seventy, said only, ‘Do you know how many sparrows are sold for two pennies?’ and went on counting the contractions with her hand on the patient's wrist. By morning the child was born and the road had been cleared. ‘I was not afraid when she said that,’ the nurse said later. ‘Not that the danger was small, but that I was counted.’ She still keeps a small card with the sparrow verse in her uniform pocket.

pm.open: God of Jacob and of Mar Yakob, you tell us not to fear, for you are with us. Strengthen us with your right hand, and teach us what to say. Amen.
share: Do not fear, for I am with you (Isaiah 41:10). What fear do I bring to him today?
Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you? (Acts 19:15). Do I use the name of Jesus, or do I belong to him?
The weapons of our warfare are not merely human (2 Corinthians 10:4). What are my weapons when I am hurt or angry?
Everyone who acknowledges me before others (Luke 12:8). Where do I stay silent about my faith?
pm.resp: Lord, we do not fear; you are with us.
interc: For the Church of the East and for all Christians in the lands where Mar Yakob lived, that they may live in peace.
For Christians who suffer persecution, that they may bear witness without fear.
For all who are afraid tonight: the sick, the lonely and those who face the storm and flood.
For catechists and teachers, that they may build up and not tear down.
For ourselves, that we may trust Christ alone.
pm.close: Father, you do not forget one sparrow. Keep us in your love and give us the courage of your martyrs and saints, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church of the East remembers Mar Yakob, a bishop of Nisibis who lived about seventeen hundred years ago. He was a man of prayer, a teacher of the Scriptures, and the teacher of the young Ephrem, who became one of the greatest poets of our tradition. Our Qurbana, with its prayer of Addai and Mari, comes from this same Church.

The first reading is God's promise to Jacob: “Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God” (Isaiah 41:10). God does not say this to the strong. He says it to a little people, even to the “worm Jacob”. He chooses the small and holds them with his right hand.

In Acts, people burned their books of magic in public. The name of Jesus is not a charm. We do not trust amulets, horoscopes or lucky days; we trust the Lord himself. If there is any such thing in our house, today is a good day to put it away.
Saint Paul tells us that our weapons are not the world's weapons. They are prayer, the word of God and love, and they are used for building up and not for tearing down (2 Corinthians 10:4, 8).

And Jesus says: “Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Luke 12:7). Not one is forgotten before God. If we acknowledge him before others, he will acknowledge us before the angels, and the Holy Spirit will teach us what to say. Let us carry this courage into the week. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember Mar Yakob, a bishop who loved to pray and to teach children. One of the boys he taught, Ephrem, grew up to write beautiful songs for God. Jesus tells us not to be afraid, because God knows every little sparrow, and he knows you even better. So when you are afraid of the dark, of exams or of storms, say: ‘Jesus, you are with me.’

intro: Theme: “Do not fear, for I am with you.”
The saint of the frontier city, the name of Jesus that is no charm, the weapons that build up, and the sparrows that are counted.

points.h: Do not fear, for I am with you
q: Do not fear, you worm Jacob, you insect Israel! I will help you, says the Lord; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.
points.apply: Give one particular fear to the Lord each evening this week.

points.h: Not a charm, but the name
q: Some take pride in chariots, and some in horses, but our pride is in the name of the Lord our God.
A number of those who practiced magic collected their books and burned them publicly; when the value of these books was calculated, it was found to come to fifty thousand silver coins.
points.apply: Put away any amulet or horoscope you trust.

sub: For building up, not for tearing down.
The teacher as Mar Yakob was.
q: The Lord is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts; so I am helped, and my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him.
Indeed, we live as human beings, but we do not wage war according to human standards; for the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power to destroy strongholds.
points.apply: Teach one prayer to one child this week.

sub: The Holy Spirit will teach you.
q: Now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to speak.
for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.
points.apply: Acknowledge your faith once, quietly and with respect, where it is usually left unsaid.

concl: God holds the small and the afraid with his right hand, and he does not forget one sparrow.
Let us trust in the name of Jesus alone and bear witness without fear.
2027-07-09.resolve: This week, give one fear to the Lord, put away one false trust, and say one word of faith.
